sections.Astrophysical Alerts:
#### IceCube-261113A: a Gold track with no significant Fermi-LAT counterpart

IceCube detected a track-like neutrino candidate on **13 November 2026 at 16:48:28.48 UTC**. The offline reconstruction gives **RA 165.45° (+0.22°/−0.16°), Dec −14.94° (+0.20°/−0.19°)**, with the quoted asymmetric intervals describing the **90% point-spread-function containment**. It entered the **Gold** alert stream and has an estimated atmospheric-background false-alarm rate of **0.2215 events yr⁻¹**. No FL16Y gamma-ray source lies inside the 90% region. This is a high-purity neutrino candidate, not a source association. The event was reported in GCN on **14 November at 16:08 UTC**. [IceCube circular](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46275).

Fermi-LAT reported on **15 November at 13:06 UTC** that its survey data show no new **>5σ** excess above 100 MeV within the IceCube 90% region. For a point source fixed at the neutrino best-fit direction with photon index 2.0, the preliminary **95% confidence** photon-flux limits above 100 MeV are **<2.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ cm⁻² s⁻¹** over the approximately 18-year mission interval, **<4.9 × 10⁻⁹ cm⁻² s⁻¹** over the month before the event, and **<9.1 × 10⁻⁸ cm⁻² s⁻¹** over the preceding day. These limits constrain one assumed spectral model; the non-detection does not establish that the neutrino lacks an electromagnetic counterpart. [Fermi-LAT follow-up](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46294).

#### GRB 261113A: bright prompt emission, an optical flash and a secure redshift

SVOM/ECLAIRs triggered on **13 November at 14:31:02 UTC**. The initial 8–120 keV image had **S/N 56.88**, and the 90% localization radius was **2.42 arcmin**, including a 2-arcmin systematic term. MXT began 131 s later and found an uncatalogued X-ray source. [Initial SVOM alert](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46244). The refined ECLAIRs analysis gives **T90 = 7.8 ± 0.1 s** in 4–120 keV. A cutoff power law fitted over 5–120 keV has index **−0.61 ± 0.05** and observed peak energy **108 ± 10 keV**; the 4–120 keV fluence is **(2.81 ± 0.09) × 10⁻⁶ erg cm⁻²**. At the measured redshift, the reported standard-cosmology estimates are **Eiso = (1.10 ± 0.09) × 10⁵³ erg** and rest-frame **Ep = 495 keV**; all quoted ECLAIRs errors are 68% intervals. Its position on the Amati plane is consistent with the authors’ Type-II/collapsar-like comparison, but that consistency is not by itself a progenitor identification. [Refined prompt analysis](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46270).

The earliest reported optical observations began **74 s after trigger**; MASTER measured an unfiltered magnitude of approximately **15.7** at 79 s, while NUTTelA-TAO measured **i′ = 16.3 ± 0.07** and **g′ = 17.2 ± 0.08 AB** at 174 s. [MASTER](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46258), [NUTTelA-TAO](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46262). VLT/X-shooter spectroscopy beginning **14 November at 00:42:17 UTC**, 10.18 h after trigger, detected the Lyman break and C II, Si II, C IV and Fe II absorption at **z = 3.580**; the acquisition image gave **r = 22.00 ± 0.06 AB** at 9.98 h. [VLT redshift](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46261). The multi-instrument sequence establishes a rapidly fading afterglow and a secure absorption redshift; detailed energetics still depend on calibration and cosmology, and no contemporaneous neutrino or gravitational-wave association was reported.

#### GRB 261114A: a long SVOM burst at z = 3.716

SVOM/ECLAIRs triggered on **14 November at 09:33:13 UTC**. The 8–120 keV image had **S/N 13.84**, the initial **90% radius was 5.91 arcmin**, and the broad single pulse had **T90 ≈ 46⁺⁶₋₉ s**. MXT found no onboard X-ray source; that instrumental non-detection does not exclude an afterglow. [Initial alert](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46267). VT identified a fading optical candidate at **RA 345.81339°, Dec −32.31699°** with a 0.50-arcsec uncertainty: at 6.45 min it measured **VT_B = 19.54 ± 0.02** and **VT_R = 18.09 ± 0.01 AB**, fading by roughly half a magnitude by 14.55 min. The photometry was not corrected for Galactic reddening. [VT follow-up](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46269).

VLT/FORS2 spectra obtained from **15 November at 03:44:31 UTC**, 18.19 h after trigger, show Lyα and narrow Si II, Si IV and C IV absorption at **z = 3.716**. The acquisition image measured **i = 22.6 ± 0.2 AB** at 18.07 h. This is a spectroscopic redshift for the afterglow; the circular does not yet provide refined prompt energetics. [VLT/FORS2](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46290).

#### GRB 261113B: a particle-classified trigger recovered as a GRB

Fermi/GBM triggered on **13 November at 19:45:55.10 UTC**, but the flight software initially classified the event as distant particles. Ground analysis instead identifies a likely long GRB at **RA 168.2°, Dec +42.4°**, with a **2.76° statistical localization uncertainty**; the event was 147° from the LAT boresight. The reclassification was reported on **14 November at 23:55 UTC**. [Fermi/GBM final localization](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46281).

Insight-HXMT/HE independently detected a multi-pulsed event at the same time. Its CsI data give **T90 = 8.0⁺³·⁵₋₆·⁰ s**, **1-s peak rate 811 counts s⁻¹** from T0+0.25 s, and **1434 total counts** in the detector’s approximately 60–900 keV deposited-energy band. These are instrumental count measurements, not a calibrated fluence. The independent detection supports the GRB reclassification, but no counterpart or redshift was reported. [Insight-HXMT](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46283).

#### EP261115a: an uncatalogued X-ray transient without an optical identification

Einstein Probe/WXT triggered on **15 November at 00:22:13 UTC**, localizing EP261115a to **RA 58.644°, Dec −44.311°** with a 3-arcmin 90% radius. FXT found an uncatalogued source at **RA 58.6217°, Dec −44.2950°**, with a **20-arcsec 90% radius** including statistical and systematic uncertainty. No X-ray flux or duration was supplied in the initial report. [Einstein Probe detection](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46282).

FRAM-Auger began at **01:25:27 UTC**, about 63 min after trigger, and found no new source in the FXT circle, reaching **R_C > 18.9 Vega at 3σ** in a 48-frame stack near 92 min. [FRAM-Auger](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46298). SVOM/VT began at **01:59:00 UTC** and obtained deeper **3σ** limits at 2.43 h of **VT_B > 23.6** and **VT_R > 23.3 AB**. [SVOM/VT](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46297). These limits exclude bright optical emission at the stated times and bands; they do not identify the X-ray source or prove the absence of an optical counterpart at other epochs or wavelengths.

#### EP261114a is reclassified as a likely stellar flare

WXT triggered on **14 November at 19:40:35.649 UTC**, initially reporting an uncatalogued transient at **RA 68.336°, Dec −3.541°** with a 3-arcmin 90% radius; FXT found a source inside that region. [Initial alert](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46284). Telemetry analysis refined the FXT position to **RA 68.3436°, Dec −3.50425°**, with an approximately 10-arcsec 90% radius, and associated it with the high-proper-motion star **UCAC4 433-006766**. The estimated 0.5–4 keV flux was **1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ erg cm⁻² s⁻¹**, corresponding to a quoted luminosity of **5.6 × 10³¹ erg s⁻¹**. The team described the event as *likely* a stellar flare; no association probability or uncertainty on the flux was supplied. [Classification update](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46291).

#### EP261006a: a delayed, brightening nuclear radio source

VLA follow-up of the **6 October** X-ray transient was reported on **13 November at 19:35 UTC**. No significant 10-GHz emission appeared at the X-ray/optical position on 9, 12 or 20 October, with a representative **3σ limit of 26 μJy**; the 20 October epoch contained a marginal approximately 3σ signal. On **31 October**, VLA securely detected **42.2 ± 4.5 μJy** at **RA 01:27:10.006, Dec +12:53:26.67**, with 0.1-arcsec uncertainty, coincident with the host-galaxy nucleus. The sequence indicates a brightening radio source, but the nuclear coincidence alone does not determine the transient mechanism. [VLA follow-up](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46255).

#### EP-WXT trigger 01709322455: the G 6-43 flare correction resolves the prior notice mismatch

A correction issued on **15 November at 14:41 UTC** confirms that the optical observations reported in GCN 46243 concerned **EP-WXT trigger 01709322455** and the star **G 6-43**. SVOM/C-GFT began on **12 November at 13:32:57.630 UTC** and followed the source for about 1.98 h; it faded in g, r and i, with the largest amplitude, approximately **0.30 mag**, in g. The color-dependent fading is consistent with a stellar-flare decay. This supersedes the incorrect trigger identifier in the earlier circular’s subject line; the corrected report still characterizes the classification as a stellar-flare interpretation. [Correction: GCN 46295](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46295).

#### GRB 261115A: a late-weekend Fermi trigger with no reported MASTER counterpart

Fermi/GBM triggered on a likely long GRB on **15 November at 22:10:53.44 UTC**. The ground localization is **RA 5.9°, Dec −31.1°**, with a **2.13° statistical uncertainty**; the event was 37° from the LAT boresight. [Fermi/GBM localization](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46299). MASTER-OAFA began imaging at **16 November 01:50:12 UTC**, approximately 3.65 h later, and reported no new optical transient in the covered fields, with individual clear-band limits reaching **19.9 mag**. [MASTER report](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46300). Because the GBM region is broad and the circular does not state complete probability coverage, this is a limited follow-up non-detection rather than evidence that the burst had no optical counterpart.

#### SN 2016coi remains radio bright a decade after explosion

ATel 18154, issued **13 November 2026 at 12:05 UTC**, reports VLA observations obtained on **30 October**: **3.5 ± 0.2 mJy at 3.32 GHz** and **1.2 ± 0.1 mJy at 9.80 GHz**, implying a spectral index **−0.96 ± 0.09**. ASKAP had also measured **8.06 ± 0.50 mJy at 0.856 GHz** on **24 December 2025**. The radio source remains coincident with the supernova position roughly ten years after explosion. These measurements establish persistent non-thermal radio emission but do not alone determine whether the late-time power arises from circumstellar interaction, a compact remnant, or another component. [ATel 18154](https://www.astronomerstelegram.org/?read=18154).
